title: A CHRISTIAN MAN WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE—AND THE CHURCH WAS BOASTING
paragraphs: A CHRISTIAN MAN WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE—AND THE CHURCH WAS BOASTING
Paul was horrified by the sexual scandal. But what he said next reveals something even more frightening: the church had learned to live comfortably beside what should have broken its heart.
Imagine the letter being opened in church.
People gather.
Believers who know the songs. Believers who know the language. Believers who can talk about grace, spiritual gifts, wisdom, freedom, and the power of God.
Then Paul's words are read aloud.
And suddenly the room gets uncomfortable.
Because somewhere among them is a man openly involved with his father's wife.
Paul does not whisper about it.
He does not dress it up.
He does not rename it so everyone can remain comfortable.
He writes:
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
In plain sense:
“Sexual immorality is actually being reported among you…”
Then comes the detail:
“ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
…so that a man has his father’s wife.
—1 Corinthians 5:1
Notice the precision.

Paul says “his father’s wife.” Scripture does not explicitly tell us that she was the man's biological mother, so we should not claim more than the text gives us. But the relationship itself was unmistakably forbidden. The Old Testament had already declared, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife” (Leviticus 18:8).
This was not a gray area.
This was not two Christians disagreeing about a secondary doctrine.
This was blatant sexual immorality inside the professing church.
Yet here is what makes the passage terrifying.
The man’s sin was not the only scandal.
The church’s response was.
Paul continues:
“καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ…”
Kai hymeis pephysiōmenoi este…
“And you are arrogant!”
The word carries the idea of being puffed up.
Inflated.
Proud.
Paul looks at a church where serious sexual sin is being tolerated and essentially asks:
Why are you puffed up?
Why aren't you grieving?
He says they should have mourned.
That changes the temperature of the entire passage.
Because biblical holiness is not supposed to produce people who enjoy discovering someone else's sin.
It produces grief.
There is a difference between mourning sin and enjoying scandal.
There is a difference between confronting someone because you love Christ and exposing someone because you love attention.
There is a difference between holiness and self-righteousness.
Paul does not sound entertained.
He sounds heartbroken.
And perhaps this is where the ancient scandal in Corinth suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because we live in a world where scandal has become entertainment.
A marriage collapses.
People watch.
A pastor falls.
People share clips.
A Christian is exposed.
Someone confesses sexual sin.
Screenshots travel faster than prayers.
And sometimes the people shouting loudest about another person's darkness have carefully hidden rooms of their own.
But 1 Corinthians 5 will not let us hide behind someone else's scandal.
It turns the light around.
It asks:
What have you learned to tolerate?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you still quote Scripture.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you raise your hands during worship while carrying something into God's presence that you have already decided you will not surrender.
Pornography.
An affair.
Secret messages.
Bitterness.
Dishonesty.
A relationship you know dishonors Christ.
A private addiction.
A double life.
A compromise you once resisted but now defend.
At first, your conscience screamed.
Then it whispered.
Then you learned how to worship over the noise.
That is one of sin's most frightening victories.
Not merely when you fall.
But when falling stops frightening you.
Not merely when you sin.
But when you become comfortable protecting what Jesus died to free you from.
Please understand what Paul is not teaching.
He is not telling Christians to become obsessed with policing unbelievers.

Later in this very chapter he makes the distinction clear. His immediate concern is someone who bears the name “brother” while persisting in serious, unrepentant sin. Paul explicitly distinguishes the church's responsibility toward those inside from God's judgment of those outside.
The church was never commissioned to stand outside the hospital screaming at sick people for being sick.
We were commissioned to proclaim the Physician.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the grave.
Calling sinners everywhere not to pretend, but to repent and believe.
And repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finds us in the darkness and we finally stop arguing with the Light.
That is why Paul's severe instruction concerning the Corinthian man must not be reduced to revenge.
His words are shocking:
“παραδοῦναι τὸν τοιοῦτον τῷ Σατανᾷ…”
“To deliver such a one to Satan…”
But keep reading.
Paul gives a purpose:
“…ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ…”
“…so that the spirit may be saved…”
—1 Corinthians 5:5
Even discipline has redemption in view.
Even confrontation is supposed to look toward salvation.
The goal is not, “Destroy this disgusting sinner.”
The goal is that sin loses its hiding place, false security collapses, repentance becomes possible, and the sinner is driven back toward the mercy of Christ.
That is an enormous difference.
Biblical church discipline is not permission for cruelty.
It is not spiritual entertainment.
It is not gossip wearing a prayer-request costume.
It is not humiliation for clicks.
It is love refusing to call spiritual poison harmless.
Imagine a doctor discovering aggressive cancer and saying:
“I don't want to make you uncomfortable, so I'll call it a personality difference.”
That would not be compassion.
A love that refuses to tell the truth when someone's destruction is approaching is not the love Scripture describes.
But neither is truth without love.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better than both sentimental tolerance and merciless condemnation.
Grace and truth meet in Him.
And that brings us to the deepest wound in this story.
The Corinthian church had apparently become capable of boasting while corruption remained among them.
Paul answers with an image everybody who understood bread would recognize:
“μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ.”
A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
Sin rarely asks permission to destroy everything at once.
It begins smaller.
One compromise.
One hidden conversation.
One image.
One lie.
One rationalization.
One secret.
One sentence:
“It's not that serious.”
Then another:
“God understands.”
Then another:
“Everybody struggles.”
And yes—God understands.
Yes—Christians struggle.
Yes—grace is greater than our sin.
But none of those glorious truths means sin should become our protected roommate.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could make peace treaties with the chains He came to break.
Paul suddenly brings the entire discussion to Christ:
“καὶ γὰρ τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐτύθη Χριστός.”
“For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”
There.
That is the center.
Not the scandalous man.
Not the embarrassed church.
Not even Paul.
Christ.
The Lamb.
The Cross.
The blood.
The sacrifice.
The possibility that guilty people can actually become clean.
Christianity does not say, “Clean yourself up so Jesus might love you.”
Christianity announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
But the grace that receives us in our filth does not celebrate leaving us there.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus breaks chains.
Jesus teaches forgiven sinners how to walk in the light.
Maybe that is why this chapter bothers us so deeply.
We would rather choose one of two comfortable lies.
Either:
“Sin doesn't really matter because God is gracious.”
Or:
“You sinned badly, so there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel destroys both.
At the Cross, God shows us that sin is so serious that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And at that same Cross, God shows us that His mercy is so astonishing that sinners who deserve judgment can be forgiven through Christ.
Your sin is more serious than your excuses tell you.
And Christ's grace is greater than your shame tells you.
Both are true.
Maybe you are reading this carrying something nobody knows.
Something happened last night.
Or five years ago.
Maybe you have begged God for forgiveness and still wake up remembering it.
Maybe you are not the person committing the scandal.
Maybe you are the person wounded by someone else's.
You were betrayed.
Cheated on.
Lied to.
Used.
Manipulated.
Humiliated.
And somebody used the language of “grace” to pressure you into pretending it didn't hurt.
That is not what this passage requires.
Grace does not call evil good.
Forgiveness does not require calling betrayal harmless.
Restoration does not mean abandoning wisdom, accountability, truth, or appropriate boundaries.
Jesus does not heal us by rewriting evil into something innocent.
He rewrites us.
That is what makes grace so breathtaking.
The Gospel does not need a sanitized past to create a redeemed future.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ was dying under criminal judgment.
Paul had persecuted the church.
Corinth was filled with people whose former lives included devastating sins, yet only one chapter later Paul could speak of their past and then say:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
There may be no more beautiful past-tense word in the Christian life.
Were.
Not because they became morally impressive enough to erase their histories.
Paul continues with what God had done:
They were washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for never becoming scandalous.
Dead people receiving life.
Dirty people being washed.
Guilty people being justified.
Captives being freed.
Prodigals coming home.
Sinners discovering that the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are stronger than the hands of their past.
So if this article exposed something hidden, do not run farther into darkness.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek trustworthy biblical accountability.
Make necessary changes.
Bring what is hidden into appropriate light.
If another person is endangered, abused, exploited, or victimized, seeking proper protection and lawful help is not a betrayal of grace.
And do not confuse repentance with merely feeling terrible.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But Peter came back to Jesus.
Repentance turns.
It stops defending darkness and starts walking toward Christ.
You may stumble on that road.
You may need help.
You may have consequences to face.
Grace does not always remove consequences.
But consequences are not proof that Christ has abandoned the repentant sinner.
Sometimes the most painful chapter of your life becomes the place where pretending finally dies.
And when pretending dies, healing can begin.
Not because strangers need the details of your private sin.
They don't.
You do not owe the internet your confession.
But perhaps those three words can become your declaration:
No more hiding from Jesus.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the Light.
And if this made you think of someone who is quietly drifting from Christ, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
Send it with love.
One share can place the Gospel in front of a person you may never realize needed it that night.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow.
Come back when compromise starts sounding reasonable.
Come back when shame tells you Jesus could never receive you.
Come back when somebody else's scandal tempts you to become proud.
And remember:
The appropriate Christian response to sin is neither applause nor self-righteous delight.
It is truth.
Grief.
Repentance.
Holiness.
Grace.
And Jesus.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But one practical way you can help Gospel-centered teaching reach more people is by supporting the work that produces and distributes it.

And comment—not to feed an algorithm with empty words, but to make the comment section a place where people see that Christians still believe repentance is possible, grace is real, and Jesus still restores sinners.
Because somewhere tonight, someone believes their scandal is the final sentence of their story.
It isn't.
The Cross stands between what you were and what Christ can make you.
And perhaps the line you need to carry away from Corinth is this:
Jesus does not expose darkness because He delights in your shame; He calls you into the light because He refuses to leave you buried where grace came to find you.
